locations.name: Chefchaouen
locations.blurb: A whole hill town painted in blue, folded into the Rif Mountains of northern Morocco. Founded in 1471 as a fortress against the Portuguese, it stayed closed to outsiders for centuries, and the blue washes over walls, steps, doors and flowerpots alike.
locations.fun_fact: Nobody agrees why it is blue. The stories run from Jewish refugees in the 1930s bringing the colour with them, to a belief that blue keeps mosquitoes off, to the simple fact that it sells.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Walk up to the ruined Spanish Mosque on the eastern hill for sunset — half an hour up, and the whole blue town is below you at once.

locations.name: Sahara at Merzouga
locations.blurb: The edge of the Sahara at Erg Chebbi, where a sea of orange dunes rises 150 m straight out of flat stony desert with no warning at all. Camel caravans go out from the village of Merzouga at the foot of them and camp between the crests.
locations.fun_fact: Erg Chebbi is only about 22 km long — a single isolated dune field, not the endless Sahara of the films, which is why you can stand on its highest crest and see hard desert on every side.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: A seasonal lake, Dayet Srji, appears west of the dunes after rain and fills with flamingos. Most visitors never look behind them.

locations.name: Casablanca
locations.blurb: Morocco's largest city and its economic engine — a working Atlantic port of art deco boulevards and glass towers rather than a tourist medina. The film was shot in Hollywood and the city has been living that down ever since.
locations.fun_fact: The Hassan II Mosque stands partly over the water, has room for 105,000 worshippers, and carries the tallest minaret in the world at 210 m, with a laser on top aimed at Mecca.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: It is one of the very few mosques in Morocco non-Muslims may enter, on guided tours several times a day — the glass floor over the Atlantic is the reason to go.

locations.name: Nairobi
locations.blurb: East Africa's business capital, a fast, green, high-altitude city of five million on the edge of the Rift Valley — and the only capital city on Earth with a full national park inside its limits.
locations.fun_fact: Lions, rhinos and giraffes range across Nairobi National Park with the city skyline directly behind them; the park is fenced on three sides and left open on the fourth so the herds can still migrate.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The elephant orphanage opens to the public for one hour a day, when the keepers bring the calves in for their milk.

locations.name: Maasai Mara
locations.blurb: 1,500 km² of open savanna in southwestern Kenya, continuous with the Serengeti across the Tanzanian border — flat gold grass, scattered acacias, and the highest density of big cats anywhere in Africa.
locations.fun_fact: Around 1.3 million wildebeest and several hundred thousand zebra cross the Mara River here between July and October, and the crossings are chaotic enough that the drownings alone feed the river's crocodiles for the year.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Balloon safaris lift off before dawn and land for breakfast on the grass — the only way to see how far the herds actually stretch.

locations.name: Mombasa
locations.blurb: Kenya's port and second city, on an island in a creek on the Indian Ocean — a Swahili trading town for a thousand years, with Arab, Portuguese, Omani and British layers stacked on top of each other in the same few streets.
locations.fun_fact: Fort Jesus changed hands at least nine times between 1631 and 1875; one Omani siege of the Portuguese garrison lasted 33 months and ended with eleven survivors.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Haller Park is a rehabilitated cement quarry — a limestone pit replanted into forest with giraffes and hippos in it, and the best argument in East Africa that industrial land can be given back.

locations.name: Dakar
locations.blurb: Perched on the westernmost tip of continental Africa, Dakar is a fast-moving Atlantic capital of markets, mosques, and the thumping mbalax music it gave the world. Colonial-era Plateau meets sea-spray corniches, with the haunting slave-trade memorial of Gorée just offshore.
locations.fun_fact: Dakar sits on the Cap-Vert peninsula, the westernmost point of mainland Africa — and lent its name to the legendary Paris–Dakar rally.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Take the short ferry to Île de Gorée for its colonial lanes and the sobering House of Slaves before the afternoon crowds arrive.

locations.name: Addis Ababa
locations.blurb: Africa's diplomatic capital and the seat of the African Union, Addis Ababa sprawls across the highlands at some 2,355 m. It's the home of 'Lucy,' Ethiopia's ancient ancestor, and a city of vast markets, incense-filled churches, and the world's original coffee culture.
locations.fun_fact: Addis Ababa's National Museum holds 'Lucy' (Dinkinesh), a 3.2-million-year-old human ancestor whose bones rewrote the story of where we come from.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Sit through a full traditional coffee ceremony — roasting, brewing, three rounds — the way Ethiopians have done for centuries.

locations.name: Banjul
locations.blurb: One of Africa's smallest capitals — about 30,000 people on a sand island at the mouth of the Gambia River, reached by bridge or ferry, with a market, a cathedral, a mosque and not much traffic.
locations.fun_fact: The whole country is essentially the river plus a few kilometres either side of it: Gambia is 50 km across at its widest and 480 km long, drawn around a waterway rather than a territory.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: The upriver boat to Kunta Kinteh Island, the old slave-trading post in the middle of the Gambia, takes most of a day and is the country's most serious visit.

locations.name: Cape Town
locations.blurb: A city wrapped around a flat-topped mountain where two oceans meet — beaches, vineyards and townships within half an hour of each other, and a skyline dominated by a 1,000 m cliff that is often wearing a cloud.
locations.fun_fact: Table Mountain is roughly six times older than the Himalayas, and its 2,200 plant species — more than the whole of the United Kingdom — grow in an area smaller than greater London.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Bo-Kaap's painted houses are a living neighbourhood, not a set. Buy something, ask before photographing doorways, and walk up to the mosque at the top for the view back over the bowl.

locations.name: Table Mountain
locations.blurb: A three-kilometre level plateau of sandstone standing over Cape Town, reached by a rotating cable car or on foot up Platteklip Gorge. The 'tablecloth' of cloud pours over its northern edge when the southeaster blows and evaporates halfway down.
locations.fun_fact: The cable car's floor rotates through 360° during the five-minute ascent, so every passenger gets the whole view without moving — and the cars carry water up for the summit buildings as ballast.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Walk down instead of riding down. Platteklip Gorge takes about 90 minutes on the way down and the light on the city is better in the late afternoon than from any photograph taken at the top.

locations.name: Camps Bay
locations.blurb: A white-sand beach on the Atlantic side of the Cape Peninsula, with the grey buttresses of the Twelve Apostles standing straight up behind it and a strip of palm trees, bars and restaurants along Victoria Road. Cape Town's sunset address, and it knows it.
locations.fun_fact: The sea here rarely gets above about 15 °C even in February: the Benguela current drags cold water up the west coast, so the beach a peninsula away in False Bay can be eight degrees warmer than this one.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Walk north along the sand and over the rocks to Glen Beach, the small cove the surfers use — the crowd thins out completely, and the view back at the Apostles catching the last light is the one the restaurants on the strip are all facing away from.

locations.name: Johannesburg
locations.blurb: Born from an 1886 gold rush, Johannesburg — 'Jozi' — is South Africa's biggest city and its restless economic engine. It's the gateway to Soweto and the Apartheid Museum, a place where the country's hardest history and its most energetic reinvention sit side by side.
locations.fun_fact: Johannesburg is often called one of the world's largest man-made urban forests — millions of trees now cover a city that sits on naturally treeless highveld.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Spend a morning at the Apartheid Museum for context, then eat and browse the industrial-chic Maboneng precinct downtown.

locations.name: Kruger National Park
locations.blurb: Nearly 20,000 km² of bushveld along South Africa's Mozambique border — the size of Wales, with 900 km of tarred road through it, which makes it one of the few great African parks you can drive yourself around in an ordinary car.
locations.fun_fact: Kruger holds the largest rhino population of any protected area on Earth, and the exact locations are a state secret: the park no longer publishes rhino counts by region, to keep them from poachers.
locations.hidden_gem_tip: Book a camp inside the gates and be on the road at opening. The first and last hour of light are when everything moves, and the gates shut hard at dusk — the fines are real.
